grammarNotes.u1: Polite Greetings & Desu/Masu: Japanese politeness is encoded in verb endings like です (desu) and ます (masu). Notice how greetings shift by time of day, and phrases like よろしくお願いします carry deep social warmth.
grammarNotes.u2: Pronouns, Particles は & の: Japanese often omits pronouns once context is clear. Use は (wa) to mark the topic and の (no) to show possession (e.g., 私の母 = my mother). Family terms also distinguish your own family (母, 父) from others' (お母さん, お父さん).
grammarNotes.u3: Numbers, Counters & Time Particle に: Japanese uses counters matched to object shapes (杯 for cups, 枚 for flat tickets, 冊 for books). Specific points in time take に (ni), while relative words like 今日 (today) and 明日 (tomorrow) do not.
grammarNotes.u4: Food, Dining & Polite Requests: Use を (o) to mark direct objects of verbs like 食べる (to eat) and 飲む (to drink). Adding お願いします (onegaishimasu) or いただけますか makes restaurant requests naturally polite.
grammarNotes.u5: I-Adjectives, Na-Adjectives & Verb Dictionary Forms: Japanese adjectives fall into い-adjectives (赤い, 大きい) and な-adjectives (静かな). Verbs end in an -u sound in dictionary form (行く, 来る, 食べる) and follow Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) order.
grammarNotes.u6: Direction Particles に・へ・で & Giving Directions: Mark destinations with に or へ, and means of transport with で (電車で = by train). The て-form connects sequential directions such as 左に曲がってください (please turn left).
grammarNotes.u7: Shopping Expressions & Potential Forms: Ask prices with いくらですか and express desire with ～たい (買いたい = want to buy). Use ～てもいいですか or potential verbs (払えますか) when asking about payment options.
grammarNotes.u8: Weather, Nature & Existence Verbs ある/いる: Use 降る (furu) for falling rain or snow and 吹く (fuku) for blowing wind. Note the distinction between 熱い (hot to the touch) and 暑い (hot weather), and between 冷たい and 寒い.
grammarNotes.u9: Health, Body Parts & Giving Advice: Describe physical states with が痛い (hurts) or 熱がある (have a fever). Use ～たほうがいい (should) and ～てください (please do) for medical advice and urgent requests.
grammarNotes.u10: Work, Study & Nominalizing Actions with こと/の: Turn verbs into nouns with こと or の to talk about hobbies and habits (音楽を聴くこと = listening to music). Mark locations of action with で (大学で勉強する).
grammarNotes.u11: Expressing Feelings & Opinions with と思う: Quote thoughts and opinions using ～と思う (I think that...) after the plain form. Note that Japanese distinguishes your own internal feelings (嬉しい) from observing others' (嬉しそうだ).
grammarNotes.u12: Past Experiences, Promises & Modifiers: Relative clauses precede the noun they modify without a relative pronoun (私がした約束 = the promise I made). Express past life experiences with ～たことがある.
grammarNotes.u13: Katakana Loanwords & Suru-Verbs: Tech vocabulary frequently uses Katakana (パソコン, アプリ) or Sino-Japanese compounds paired with する (検索する = to search, 更新する = to update).
grammarNotes.u14: Cultural Terms, Passive Voice & Honorifics: Passive forms (～られる, e.g., 歌い継がれている) are common when describing traditions and heritage. Notice the honorific prefix お/ご in hospitality terms like お客様 and ご挨拶.
grammarNotes.u15: Logical Connectors & Conditionals (ば・たら・なら): Link clauses smoothly using ので/から (because), しかし (however), ～のに/～けれども (although), and conditionals like ～ば or ～たら (if). Contrast alternatives with ～の代わりに (instead of).
grammarNotes.u16: Business Japanese & Formal Sino-Japanese (漢語): Workplace discourse relies heavily on two-kanji compound nouns (戦略, 契約, 交渉) and humble/respectful phrasing to maintain professional harmony.
grammarNotes.u17: Academic Prose & Objective Style (だ・である): Scientific writing often uses the plain declarative style (である), passive constructions, and precise compound nouns (仮説, 実験, 精密さ) to convey objectivity.
grammarNotes.u18: Causative, Potential & Sustainability Discourse: Discuss environmental cause and effect with によって (by means of), ～につながる (leads to), and causative/transitive verbs (守る, 削減する, 再生する).
grammarNotes.u19: Civic Vocabulary & Formal Obligations: Legal and civic discourse uses expressions like ～なければならない (must), ～に基づき (based on), and ～を保障する (guarantees) to articulate rights and institutional duties.
grammarNotes.u20: Critical Debate & Hedging Expressions: Structure persuasive analysis with ～を踏まえて (taking into account), ～にもかかわらず (nevertheless), and ～という観点から (from the perspective of).
grammarNotes.u21: Aesthetics, Literary Expressions & Nuance: Japanese literary criticism draws on evocative compounds (象徴性, 余韻, 崇高) and delicate aspectual nuances like ～ていく and ～てくる to trace shifting emotion.
grammarNotes.u22: Philosophical Discourse & Abstract Nominalization: Express abstract concepts using suffixes like ～性 (nature/quality), ～観 (view/outlook), and formal structures such as ～とは何か (what is...?) and ～を通じて (through).
grammarNotes.u23: Proverbs (ことわざ), Four-Character Idioms (四字熟語) & Set Phrases: Authentic Japanese relies on vivid proverbs (七転び八起き, 継続は力なり) and somatic idioms (行間を読む, 心を入れ替える) rather than literal translations of English idioms.
grammarNotes.u24: Diplomatic, Legal & High-Register Keigo: Treaties and formal speeches employ literary grammar such as ～にもかかわらず (notwithstanding), ～に鑑み (in light of), したがって (consequently), and deferential formulas like 恐れ入りますが.
grammarNotes.u25: Rhetorical Precision & Native-Level Mastery: Master C2 nuance through refined qualifiers (疑いの余地なく, 同様に, 総合的に見て), rhythmic parallelism, and effortless command of register from poetic understatement to persuasive clarity.
